 MEMPHIS, Tenn. - 
 It is almost time to, well, change the time.
 Daylight saving time comes to an end at 2 a.m. Sunday, meaning we get an extra hour of sleep on Halloween night, but the sun will rise and set an hour earlier.
 FOX13 has reported several times about the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent year-round.
 If passed, this piece of legislation would mean the sunsets before 5 p.m. would be a thing of the past. But it would introduce sunrises after 8 a.m., which raises concerns among lawmakers.
 Let's take a look at what that would actually look like in Memphis.
 With the upcoming time change, the earliest sunset of the year in Memphis will occur in early December, at 4:47 p.m. But, if we did not "fall back," the earliest the sun would set is 5:47 p.m.
 What about sunrises?
 The latest sunrise of the year actually occurs on the final day of daylight saving this weekend — Halloween morning — at 7:20 a.m. The time change this weekend moves that an hour earlier to 6:21 a.m. on Sunday morning.
 But under the Sunshine Protection Act, that reset would not happen, and sunrises would keep getting later and later until early January—when the sun would not rise until 8:09 a.m.
 FOX13 reported earlier this month that several lawmakers along with President Trump have supported the passage of the Sunshine Protection Act in the Senate.
 Democratic Representative Frank Pallone of New Jersey is one of those in support of the bill.
 "Taking this action will increase the sunshine hours in the evening, allowing many Americans to leave work for more sunlight in the winter months," Pallone said.
 The President has commented on the issue before, saying, "As crazy as it sounds, when you have light, you have." You have much less crime... He shouldn't be holding it. It's an issue that people want."
 But not all lawmakers agree.
 FOX13 also reported Arkansas Senator Tom Cotton opposes the bill, to which the president posted Cotton's personal cell phone number on social media, urging people to call him and demand he support it.
 The Republican senator responded in a post of his own, stating in part, "Arkansans don't want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I'll always put Arkansas first."
 That is a big reason why previous experiences with permanent daylight saving time have failed.
 In January 1974, under President Richard Nixon, the U.S. enacted the Emergency Daylight Time Energy Conservation Act in an effort to save fuel and electricity.
 Its approval rating quickly plummeted 30 percent in a matter of months after children were injured or killed as a result of traffic accidents during dark winter morning commutes. President Gerald Ford repealed the law less than a year after it was enacted.
 The Sunshine Protection Act has been in the hands of the Senate since July, where there is currently no floor vote scheduled to put the bill into action.
